title: Food delivery order lifecycle
idea: A food delivery design is one order moving through a fixed chain of statuses, where each status may be set only by the actor who owns that step.
points: Three actors drive one order: customer places, restaurant cooks, partner delivers.
Each `Status` records which `Actor` may move the order into it.
Status changes are events: listeners notify the app and dispatch a rider.

steps.caption: The customer places order A-42 from one restaurant's menu. It starts as `PLACED`.
The restaurant accepts. Only `RESTAURANT` may set `ACCEPTED`, so the move is allowed.
The status change fires an event. The customer's app listener shows the new status.
The partner tries to mark the food ready. `READY` belongs to the restaurant, so it is refused.
The restaurant marks it `READY`. A listener reacts by asking the assigner for a rider.
The assigner picks a free partner and sends the pickup. `FoodOrder` never knows the assigner exists.
The partner sets `PICKED_UP`, then `DELIVERED`. Each change notifies the customer.

code.title: Who may move the order
code.caption: Six attempts by three actors. Wrong actors, and any move after `DELIVERED`, are refused; accepted changes reach the listeners.

walk.text: Three actors. Each one calls `advance` for its own step.
The enum lists statuses in order and stores who may set each one.
The listener contract: one method, so lambdas can implement it.
`advance` finds the next status and refuses an actor who does not own it.
Only after the change does the order notify every listener. Real code often notifies after releasing the lock.
The app hears every change; the rider listener reacts only to `READY`.

pitfalls: Never let any caller set any status; tie each transition to its owning actor.
Notify listeners only after the status change succeeds, never before the check.
Keep partner assignment outside `FoodOrder`; the order should not know how riders are chosen.

quiz.q: What is the first line `OrderFlowDemo` prints after `app: A-42 ACCEPTED`?
quiz.code:
// moves: RESTAURANT, PARTNER, RESTAURANT, ...
// order is now ACCEPTED; next status is READY
quiz.why: The second move is by `PARTNER`. The next status, `READY`, is owned by `RESTAURANT`, so `advance` throws before anything changes.

takeaway: One order, an ordered status enum, each step owned by one actor.

starters: How should the system pick which delivery partner gets the order?
Where would a cancellation with a refund fit in this design?
Why not use the State pattern with one class per status?
